source.title: Multilingual Amnesia: On the Transferability of Unlearning in Multilingual LLMs
source.authors: Alireza Dehghanpour Farashah; Aditi Khandelwal; Marylou Fauchard; Zhuan Shi; Negar Rostamzadeh; Golnoosh Farnadi

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether unlearning effects transfer across languages in Aya-Expanse-8B, a multilingual setting relevant to the claim that language changes alone can expose targeted knowledge.
record.gate_note: The paper does not test fine-tuning attacks, activation-direction ablation, quantization, jailbreaks, or prompt rephrasing. It does test cross-language querying after single-language unlearning. TOFU heatmap values are ratios of post-unlearning forget-set probability to the fine-tuned baseline; higher values indicate more probability remains. Reported examples and SeeGULL results are also included. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: In a multilingual setting, the authors unlearn TOFU facts in one language with GradDiff, GradDiff-KL or NPO. They then measure how much forget-set answer probability remains when the model is queried in nine other languages (Aya-Expanse-8B). That bears directly on whether querying in another language exposes the targeted knowledge (version E).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that data unlearning is predominantly language-specific, with limited and asymmetric transfer. Syntactic distance is the most predictive factor (r≈0.35–0.40). Transfer patterns are largely consistent across methods (heatmap correlations 0.77–0.92). Concept (stereotype) unlearning in English propagates broadly across languages. Unlearning in one language is insufficient to guarantee forgetting in others.
record.recipe_differences: Uses multilingual GradDiff, GradDiff-KL, and NPO experiments on translated TOFU and SeeGULL datasets; evaluates cross-language transfer rather than the recovery attacks in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Cross-language effects vary by unlearning method, source language, target language, and dataset. The paper reports asymmetric transfer; concept-unlearning effects differ from data-unlearning patterns.

fits_no_version.finding: SeeGULL concept unlearning of stereotypes in English reduces biased-answer rates across all evaluated languages, for both GradDiff-KL and NPO. Transfer from other source languages varies, and Japanese gains neutral answers regardless of source.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Behavioural (concept/bias) unlearning in one language propagates to other languages in multilingual LLMs.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The paper notes that translated benchmarks may contain imperfections and that evaluation metrics have limitations. Several cross-language behavioral results are shown as plots rather than tabulated values; TOFU probability ratios are not direct answer-accuracy rates. General capability is assessed with perplexity, but the claim's recovery attacks are not tested.
record.rows_left_out: The full TOFU heatmaps contain many additional source-language/target-language cells; only English-source cells and explicitly discussed asymmetric examples were extracted to keep the record focused on the claim and within the row limit. Additional SeeGULL source-language plots in Figures 13a–13r were omitted; the text reports that transfer varies by language pair and that Japanese often shows increased neutral responses.

untested.parts: No test of near-chance accuracy on a hazardous-knowledge benchmark, and no robustness check against standard attacks beyond switching the query language.
No relearning or fine-tuning attack after unlearning.
No activation-direction ablation or representation analysis of blocking versus deletion.
Only cross-language querying is tested. Same-language rephrasing, jailbreaks and in-context information are not tested.
No method is proposed or tested as robust to recovery attacks.

missing.what: In-language (diagonal) forget ratios and retain-model PF levels, needed as the reference for cross-language persistence. Examples: GradDiff EN→EN 0.00; NPO EN→EN 0.26 (incomplete forgetting even in-language); retain-model PF about 0.08–0.13 (about 0.31 in Hindi).
Truth Ratio Forget in each evaluation language, a second forgetting measure beyond raw probability.
Cross-language persistence for non-English source languages. Examples: GradDiff-KL ID→EN 0.06 versus EN→ID 0.19; NPO ratios of 0.80–0.99 off-diagonal for most sources.

Qualitative examples. NPO EN-unlearned model answers 'Kuwait' correctly in French and Indonesian, whereas GradDiff EN→FR forgets. Unlearning in Indonesian removes knowledge from English, but the reverse does not hold.
Utility after unlearning: mC4 perplexity increase (avg Δ 0.55 for EN-unlearned) and retain-set probability ratios.

record.verdict_notes: The base model was fine-tuned on TOFU in all ten languages. Each language therefore holds its own learned copy of the forget facts, so cross-language persistence may reflect separate per-language memorization rather than 'hidden' knowledge recovered from a shared store. The measure is normalized answer probability, not accuracy. NPO is the method with the most persistence, but it also forgets least in-language (EN ratio 0.26), which inflates its apparent cross-language 'recovery'. The cross-language failure also bears implicitly on A: in-language unlearning succeeds with modest utility cost, but a simple language switch often defeats it. Not labelled separately.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test whether targeted accuracy is near chance while general ability is retained and simple attacks fail to recover knowledge.
No post-unlearning fine-tuning on unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten examples.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis testing whether unlearning blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
Tests evaluation in other languages after unlearning in one language, but not rephrasing within a language, jailbreaks, or in-context information.
Does not propose or test a method against the recovery attacks in the claim.
